clue.text: Superb conductor, he manages to restrain piano

indicators.note: to restrain means the one piece holds the other inside it, as a captor holds a prisoner

parts.note: a coper is one who copes, someone who manages
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Praise for an orchestra's leader who keeps the piano player in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superb conductor' reads as a maestro, but it means a metal that conducts electricity extremely well.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal is prized in wiring because it carries electric current with very little resistance.

clue.text: He hammers last Aussie mate left in

indicators.note: in means the single letter is placed inside the Australian word for a friend

parts.note: cobber is Australian slang for a friend or mate

explanation.surface: A man pounds away at the final thing while his Australian pal is let inside.
explanation.walkthrough: A last is the foot-shaped block a shoemaker works on, so 'last' here is a noun, not 'finally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe mender nails soles and heels onto footwear held on a wooden or iron last.

clue.text: Tracy's not taking sides in change

indicators.note: not taking sides means the first and last letters, the word's sides, are dropped

parts.note: the actor Spencer Tracy's first name is Spencer

explanation.surface: An actor stays neutral in some shift of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not taking sides' suggests neutrality, but it strips the outer letters from the Hollywood star's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Small change in British coins is counted in pennies, whose plural form this is.

clue.text: Meanie comic is weenier comic

indicators.note: comic in its sense of funny or absurd signals that the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stingy comedian is described as somewhat tinier than another comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernie Wise was half of the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise; his on-screen persona was famously tight with money.
explanation.definitionFit: The British comedian's stage character was a notorious skinflint, mocked for never paying for anything.

clue.text: Several lights here ruin other non-British football broadcast live

indicators.note: ruin tells us to wreck the order of the letters that follow and rebuild them

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: non-British means the letter B, the abbreviation for British, is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Foreign football shown live on television spoils other things.
explanation.walkthrough: The full saying is 'money is the root of all evil'; several answers in the grid are kinds of money, hence 'Several lights here'. 'Broadcast' merely completes the picture of televised football.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb blames cash for every wrong, and many grid entries name forms of cash.

clue.text: A drunk forward is better than a drunk back

indicators.note: back says the whole phrase before it is read in reverse order

parts.note: to top something is to beat it, so tops means is better than
a sot is a habitual drunkard

explanation.surface: A riddle comparing a drunk going forward with one going backward.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer read forwards is a drunk; read backwards it spells TOPS SOT, 'is better than a drunk'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tosspot is an old word for a heavy drinker, one who tosses off pots of ale.

clue.text: Not much warmth there after MP struck leader

indicators.note: struck leader means the first letter is struck off

parts.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament, so a member

explanation.surface: Things cooled after a politician hit the party chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struck leader' looks like violence against a party head but means deleting the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A dying coal from a fire gives off only a faint glow of heat.

clue.text: See 4 across
He may dip his 24 in to find old coin

definitions.meaning: 24 is the answer at 24 across, a joint of the arm: a parent checks bathwater by dipping it in
a sixpence of Tudor times, or a shilling, once bore this name

explanation.walkthrough: The 24 is the joint answer at 24 across; someone testing a baby's bath dips it in to judge the temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tries water temperature is one who tests; the old coin was a debased Tudor shilling.

clue.text: No movement without altering street first

indicators.note: first says the abbreviation for street comes at the front

parts.note: as is means unchanged, without altering anything

explanation.surface: A traffic jam where the road stays as it was before.
explanation.definitionFit: Stasis is a state of equilibrium or inactivity where nothing moves or changes.

clue.text: Outlaw with forged tokens promises to pay

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it

indicators.note: forged in its sense of faked tells us the letters are counterfeited into a new order

explanation.surface: A criminal with counterfeit tokens makes pledges.
explanation.walkthrough: British banknotes carry the words 'I promise to pay the bearer on demand', hence the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Each paper currency note bears the Bank of England's printed pledge to pay its holder.

clue.text: Restaurant's short of water, most of it 1 across

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the second piece is taken away

parts.note: a brasserie is an informal French-style restaurant
Lake Erie is a body of water

explanation.surface: An eatery runs low on water, most of its supply turning to metal.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 across' refers to the answer at 1 across, the metal; this alloy is mostly that metal, mixed with zinc.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow alloy is made of copper with a smaller share of zinc.

clue.text: Place in Belgium's not the same after bum goes east

indicators.note: not the same says the remaining letters end up in a different arrangement
goes means the letters of bum depart from the country's name

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A Belgian location is altered after some layabout heads off eastward.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking B, U and M from BELGIUM leaves ELGI; adding E and rearranging gives the city. 'Place in Belgium' looks like the whole definition, but 'Belgium' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Liège is a large city in the French-speaking Wallonia region of Belgium.

clue.text: Scotch reuse plug or stick

indicators.note: to scotch is to quash or wreck, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scot advises reusing an electrical plug, or else gluing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' looks like a nationality or a whisky, but it is the verb meaning to wreck.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyanoacrylate adhesive bonds things almost instantly, sticking them firmly together.

clue.text: Sets up a classic day — it's about to start

indicators.note: to start says the word for about goes at the beginning

parts.note: re means about or concerning
dies is Latin, a classical language, for day

explanation.surface: Someone prepares a traditional celebration that is about to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' points to Latin, the language of the classics. The answer is also slang for cash, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: To ready something is to prepare it, and this is the third-person form, matching sets up.

clue.text: Distributing this wealth with it may be ineffectual

indicators.note: distributing means the letters are spread around and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sharing out riches may prove useless.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer plus IT can be rearranged to spell INEFFECTUAL, a composite anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluence is abundance of money and possessions, prosperity.

clue.text: Two plus eleven minus one, amazingly

definitions.text: Two plus eleven minus one, amazingly

indicators.note: amazingly suggests something astonishing happens to the letters, which are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, the letters to be removed from the pool

explanation.surface: A sum that adds up surprisingly well.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of TWO and ELEVEN, rearranged, give the answer plus ONE; the sum itself also equals the answer, so the whole clue defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plus eleven makes thirteen, and taking one away leaves a dozen.

clue.text: Former PM's retreat reduced Osborne's remit

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: reduced means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: Chequers is the British Prime Minister's country residence

explanation.surface: An ex-premier's country house was cut down to size by the Chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: George Osborne was Chancellor of the Exchequer, the UK finance minister, when this puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK treasury department was the area the Chancellor George Osborne was responsible for.

clue.text: Sweet FA rejected short cut

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the two letters are turned round
cut means the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: terse means short or curt

explanation.surface: Sweet Fanny Adams turned down for a brief haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet FA' is British slang for nothing at all, but 'Sweet' is the definition: AFTERS is British for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage the course after the main meal is the sweet or pudding.

clue.text: Married couple employs small potty in front

indicators.note: in front says the first pieces go before the word for employs

parts.note: PO is a chamber pot, the French pot de chambre shortened
to employ is to use, so employs means uses

explanation.surface: A husband and wife use a little toilet up front.
explanation.definitionFit: Husband and wife are each a spouse, so together they form a pair of them.

clue.text: Lay clues out at care centre

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: centre means only the middle letters are taken

explanation.surface: Someone sets out clues at a care home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' looks like a verb, but it is an adjective meaning not clerical.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay people are those outside the clergy, so non-religious or worldly.

clue.text: Spades bent piece, not 9

parts.note: S is the card-game abbreviation for spades

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A card suit with a twisted coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 refers to the answer at 9 across, paper money; this is money in coin, not paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Specie is money in the form of coins rather than paper currency notes.

clue.text: Bad news in Cape shows inexperience

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters go inside the word for cape

parts.note: ras is an Arabic-derived word for a headland or cape, as in Ras Tanura

indicators.note: bad means corrupted, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bad news from the Cape reveals naivety.
explanation.definitionFit: Rawness is greenness, being new to something without experience.

clue.text: Outcome of paparazzo's rude pic?

definitions.meaning: a photograph taken upward, as an intrusive photographer might snap up a skirt

explanation.definitionFit: The final result of something is its upshot; read as two words it is a photo taken upwards.

clue.text: Thump 23, say, for one of our old 9

parts.note: to pound is to thump
23 is the answer at 23 down, which said aloud is DOH, a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Hitting money, perhaps, to obtain an old currency note.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is 23 down, whose sound is 'doh', the first note of the sol-fa scale. The British paper pound was replaced by a coin in 1988.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's one-pound paper currency was withdrawn in favour of a coin.

clue.text: Maggie T's ultimate foreign secretary's emolument?

definitions.text: Maggie T's ultimate foreign secretary's emolument?

parts.words: Maggie T's ultimate foreign secretary's emolument?
parts.note: Margaret Thatcher's last foreign secretary was Douglas Hurd: his first name shortened plus his surname's initial, run together, is slang for pay

explanation.walkthrough: Douglas Hurd was the final foreign secretary under Margaret Thatcher; the clipped name and initial read as a single slang word for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for money, as pay or wages, a playful emolument named after Douglas Hurd.

clue.text: Formal greeting in Spanglish joint?

parts.note: Spanglish mixes Spanish with English, so the Spanish article el is put in front
a bow is a formal greeting

explanation.surface: A polite salutation delivered in a mixture of Spanish and English.
explanation.walkthrough: EL is Spanish for 'the', BOW is English: a 'Spanglish' phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint in the middle of the arm where it bends.

clue.text: Banks lose thousands investing euros in oil source

indicators.note: investing means clothing or surrounding, so one piece is wrapped around another
lose means the letter is dropped

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for thousand
E is the symbol for euros

explanation.surface: Banks shed thousands by putting money into an oil venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investing' reads as finance but means surrounding; BANS (banks less K) goes round E.
explanation.definitionFit: Soya and castor beans are pressed to yield cooking and industrial oils.

clue.text: He's a believer in India's contribution to growth industries

indicators.note: contribution to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An Indian believer helps economic expansion.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of the majority faith of India hold Hindu beliefs.

clue.text: Insist I put frying pan outside

indicators.note: outside means the criticism word wraps around the jumbled letters

parts.note: to pan is to criticise harshly, to slate

indicators.note: frying means cooked up, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone demands a frying pan be put outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frying pan' looks like one object, but 'frying' is the anagram signal and 'pan' means criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: To stipulate is to demand something as a condition, insisting on it.

clue.text: Cuts little bits of enamel article into flower

indicators.note: into means the article is inserted into the river

parts.note: a flower here is something that flows, a river: the Tees in north-east England
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Someone slices pieces of enamel decoration into a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is crossword shorthand for a river (one that flows); the Tees is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby cutting its first teeth through the gums, whose surfaces are enamel.

clue.text: Regular features of start-up sites in banks

indicators.note: regular features means every other letter is picked from the words that follow

explanation.surface: Regular content of new company websites appears at banks.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial institutions that hold money for others, such as trust companies.
